intro: A campaign slogan loses an election because its third item is the wrong shape. A will goes to court over one comma. A text message with every word spelled correctly still says the opposite of what its writer meant. None of these problems is about ideas. They are about the machinery of the sentence: how its parts fit together, and how the marks between words tell a reader what the writer intended. This unit opens that machinery up and shows you how it works.

Grammar here is not a list of rules to be punished for breaking. It is a set of tools writers use to make sentences that hold together, carry exact meaning and sound like a person. You will learn to see phrases and clauses, to make the parts of a list match, to keep verbs and pronouns pointed at the right words, and to use semicolons, colons, dashes, commas, hyphens, quotation marks, ellipses and brackets for what each one actually does. You will also learn which so-called rules were never real, and when a good writer breaks a convention on purpose.

By the end you will be able to take a real, messy draft, yours or anyone's, and edit it in passes until every sentence says exactly one thing clearly. You will be able to quote a source honestly, cite it in MLA style, and explain to another reader why a comma belongs where you put it. Most of all, you will read your own sentences the way a stranger will, because every piece of writing goes out into the world without its writer standing next to it.
bigQuestion: How do the structure of a sentence and the marks inside it carry meaning a reader can trust when the writer is not there to explain?

timeline.t: Aristophanes of Byzantium, a librarian in Alexandria, proposes dots to mark pauses in Greek texts
The Venetian printer Aldus Manutius uses the semicolon in a printed book, and the mark spreads
Samuel Johnson publishes his Dictionary of the English Language, fixing many spellings
Noah Webster publishes his American Dictionary, settling American spellings like color and center
Charles Dickens opens A Tale of Two Cities with a chain of parallel clauses
Emily Dickinson writes poems punctuated almost entirely with dashes
Lincoln's Gettysburg Address ends with three parallel phrases: of, by and for the people
The Fowler brothers publish The King's English, a guide to usage for ordinary writers
William Strunk Jr. prints The Elements of Style for his Cornell students
H. W. Fowler's Modern English Usage sorts real rules from superstitions
The Modern Language Association publishes its first style sheet for citations
The ninth edition of the MLA Handbook is published, with rules for citing web sources

words.d: a group of words that acts as one unit but has no subject and verb of its own
a clause that can stand alone as a complete sentence
a clause with a subject and verb that cannot stand alone
a participle plus its attached words, used to describe a noun
a noun plus a participle that describes the whole sentence
matching grammatical form for parts of a sentence that do the same job
the noun a pronoun stands for
a modifier whose intended subject is missing from the sentence
the mark that joins two independent clauses or separates list items containing commas
describing a clause that adds extra information and is set off by commas
three spaced periods showing where words were cut from a quotation
a short note in parentheses, usually author and page, showing a source

test.q: Which group of words is a clause?
choices: the tall kid in the hoodie
test.why: Since the bell rang has a subject (bell) and a verb (rang); the others are phrases.

test.q: 'Exhausted by the hike, the tent was set up quickly.' What is the error?
choices: A dangling modifier: the tent was not exhausted
test.why: The people who were exhausted are missing from the sentence; the phrase falls on the tent.

choices: The job involves lifting, driving and to file reports.
The job involves lifting, driving and you file reports.
The job involves lifting, driving and filing reports.
The job involves to lift, driving and filing.
test.why: Three -ing words match. The others mix a to-verb or a clause into the list.

test.q: 'Each of the students (has / have) a locker.' Which is correct?
choices: Have, because the verb agrees with the nearest noun
test.why: Each is the subject and takes a singular verb; students sits inside a prepositional phrase.

test.q: 'When Priya saw Dana, she waved.' What is the problem?
choices: The pronoun she could refer to either Priya or Dana
Waved does not agree with she
test.why: Two possible antecedents for one pronoun leave the reader unsure who waved.

test.q: Which sentence uses only correctly to mean the writer told nobody else?
choices: I only told Sam the secret.
I told only Sam the secret.
Only I told Sam the secret.
I told Sam the only secret.
test.why: Only describes the word beside it; next to Sam it limits who was told.

test.q: Which sentence has a comma splice?
choices: The rain stopped; we went outside.
The rain stopped, and we went outside.
The rain stopped, we went outside.
After the rain stopped, we went outside.
test.why: Two independent clauses joined by only a comma is a comma splice.

test.q: Which sentence uses a colon correctly?
choices: She wanted: rest, food and quiet.
She wanted rest: food and quiet.
She wanted rest, food: and quiet.
She wanted three things: rest, food and quiet.
test.why: The words before the colon form a complete sentence that the list then delivers.

test.q: 'Students who miss the deadline lose points.' What does the lack of commas mean?
choices: Only students who miss the deadline lose points
test.why: No commas means the clause is restrictive: it narrows students to those who miss the deadline.
Fire-damaged is a compound modifier before the noun; no hyphen after an -ly adverb or after the noun.

test.q: Which line of dialogue is punctuated correctly?
test.why: The comma goes inside the quotation marks and the speaker tag begins lowercase.

test.q: In American style, what marks go around a quotation inside a quotation?
test.why: Nested quotations take single marks inside the outer double marks.

test.q: What does an ellipsis in a quotation show?
choices: That the writer added a word
That there is an error in the original
test.why: Three spaced periods mark a cut in a quotation.

test.q: How is the title of a book shown in an essay?
test.why: Long, standalone works such as books are italicized; short works take quotation marks.

test.q: What must every MLA in-text citation match?
choices: A footnote at the bottom of the page
A note in the paper's introduction
A full entry on the Works Cited page
A quotation earlier in the paper
test.why: The short citation points to a full entry in the alphabetized list at the end.

write.prompt: Take a paragraph you wrote earlier this year and edit it using this unit. Then write a short explanation making this claim: the edited version says what I meant more clearly than the original. Use at least three specific changes as evidence (a comma, a parallel list, a fixed modifier, a semicolon) and explain how each changes what a reader understands.
tips: Claim: state plainly that the edited paragraph is clearer, and say for whom (a reader who was not there).
Evidence: quote the original sentence and the edited sentence side by side for each change.
Reasoning: for each pair, name the rule (restrictive comma, parallel structure, dangling modifier) and say what a reader would have misread before.
The other side: admit one place where the original sounded more natural, and say why you kept or changed it.
End by naming the one error you make most often and the test you will use to catch it.
